posts.name: Ben Woodward, CFA
posts.text:
Simply : a vol $VIX spike = spring compresses. FAST vol collapse = spring snaps. Only a FAST snap is a good buy signal. The speed of the vol collapse back from high vol matters, not just that it falls. A spike by itself just tells you fear is rising. It tells you nothing about whether the fuel will be released fast enough to matter. You're waiting for the release, not the compression.
 
Here's why:
 
Fast vol collapse = forced buying in a burst
• When volatility spikes, traders get caught short "Delta" (they're short stock as a hedge).
• If vol then collapses quickly, all those traders are forced to buy back stock at roughly the same time — a big, concentrated burst of buying.
• That burst is what creates the sharp, meaningful bottom and the strong rebound. 
Slow vol decline = buying gets spread out and wasted
• If vol just grinds lower slowly, the forced Delta buying happens in small trickles over weeks or months.
• Each little bit of buying gets absorbed by sellers. There's no concentrated "wall" of demand.
• The "potential energy" never gets released all at once — it leaks out harmlessly. 
The analogy: Think of it like a compressed spring. A vol spike compresses the spring (builds potential energy). A fast release snaps the market upward. A slow release just lets the spring uncoil gently with no pop.
 
So the sequence that actually matters for a real bottom is:
1. Vol spikes hard (panic, fear, implied vol expands)
2. Vol collapses fast (fear drains quickly)
3. Forced Delta buybacks hit all at once → sharp rally off the low 
A slow vol fade after a spike is not enough — it means the buying fuel gets dribbled out instead of detonating. That's why "calm grinding declines" (like much of 2022) are so hard to bottom from: no spike, no fast collapse, no concentrated buyback burst.

🚨 UPDATE sur Riemann et elle est énorme 

Hier, Levent Alpöge, mathématicien chez Anthropic, annonçait avoir trouvé une preuve avec Claude. C'était une revendication, personne n'avait encore vérifié

Aujourd'hui, la Lean FRO et la Mathlib Initiative, les deux organisations derrière Lean et sa bibliothèque de maths, publient une déclaration commune : « We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct »

EN 24 HEURES !! 

Elles écrivent avoir « full confidence » dans la preuve et félicitent Alpöge

Après 167 ans cest le plus gros morceau des maths qui tombe, alors que tout le monde le voyait encore résister 30-50 ans. 

1. Ce qui a changé en 24h

Hier je vous disais que personne hors de son cercle n'avait confirmé que le code compile, ni que le théorème final dit exactement ce que dit l'hypothèse de Riemann

Les deux points sont réglés. Des dizaines de personnes ont recompilé la bibliothèque de leur côté et obtenu le même fichier de preuve, sans aucune erreur

Et l'énoncé démontré est bien celui de Mathlib, qui avait déjà été relu par des experts de Lean et de théorie des nombres

2. Comment ils ont vérifié

La preuve fait 17 millions de lignes de Lean et ne dépend directement que de Mathlib

La communauté a isolé l'énoncé de Riemann dans un fichier à part, qui n'importe que Mathlib, puis l'a comparé au théorème d'Alpöge avec deux outils indépendants, comparator et con-leche. Les deux confirment que c'est exactement le même énoncé

La preuve a ensuite été passée dans plusieurs vérificateurs, dont le noyau officiel de Lean, con-leche et con-ron, plus d'autres écrits par des tiers dans d'autres langages

Détail très fort : con-leche et con-ron ont eux-mêmes une preuve formelle qu'ils ne peuvent pas accepter une fausse preuve. Ça répond à la crainte d'une faille dans la logique de Lean que la preuve aurait pu exploiter

3. Claude des deux côtés

Andrew Sutherland, du MIT, publie tous ses fichiers de vérification. Et ses contrôles ont été lancés avec Claude Code

Sur sa page : les 175 187 modules compilent, la preuve n'utilise que les trois axiomes standard de Lean, et nanoda, un noyau indépendant écrit en Rust, accepte la preuve complète

Donc Claude a aidé à trouver la preuve, et Claude a aidé à la vérifier. Avec des outils indépendants à chaque étape. 

Pour le million du Clay Institute, les règles demandent une publication dans une revue reconnue, deux ans d'attente puis une acceptation générale par la communauté. Et Anthropic n'a fait aucune communication officielle

Dodd-Frank passed in July 2010 at 2,319 pages, and the banks wrote most of it. That sentence sounds conspiratorial until you read the lobbying disclosures. JPMorgan Chase spent $7.1 million lobbying during the bill's drafting phase. Goldman Sachs dispatched former employees throughout Treasury and the Fed, the same agencies tasked with writing the implementing regulations. The revolving door spun so fast it blurred into a single continuous institution.

Regulatory capture works like this: the regulator depends on the regulated industry for technical knowledge, career advancement, and institutional prestige. The industry therefore shapes the rules it nominally must follow. Dodd-Frank handed regulators 400 separate rulemaking requirements, each one a drafting opportunity for bank lawyers to define what their own compliance looks like.

The result protected you from nothing while erecting walls against anyone who might actually compete with Citigroup. Community banks collapsed from 7,085 in 2010 to under 4,500 by 2024, crushed under compliance costs that a trillion-dollar balance sheet absorbs casually but a $200 million regional bank cannot. The big got bigger. Concentration in the top five banks rose from 44% of total assets in 2010 to over 54% by 2026.

Complexity is a moat. Every page of regulation you cannot afford to decode is a page written against you and for the incumbents who can. Free market thinkers have identified this process more than a century ago, and the math never changes: when government controls the terms of market entry, the largest existing players control government.

Dodd-Frank's defenders said it disciplined Wall Street. Wall Street's stock prices recovered within three years, bonus pools swelled by 2013, and the five largest banks emerged structurally dominant in ways 2008 never threatened to produce on its own.

You are living through one of the rarest statistical events in modern financial history.

Today, the VIX hit 32.

Most retail investors see a 30+ VIX and panic. But if you study market history and derivatives research, a VIX crossing 30 is one of the rarest and most critical macro signals in finance

In normal markets, the VIX lives between 15 and 20. A VIX  above 30 only happens in about 5% of all trading sessions in history. 

• 1997: Asian Financial Crisis 
• 1998: Russian Default & LTCM Collapse 
• 2000–2001: Dot-Com Bust 
• 2002: Enron & WorldCom Scandals 
• 2008: Great Financial Crisis 
• 2011: U.S. Credit Rating Downgrade 
• 2020: COVID-19 Global Shock 
• April 2025: Tariff & Trade War Repricing 
• March 2026: Geopolitical Escalation

What do all of these have in common? Forced margin liquidations and structural repricing.

But don't mistake extreme fear for an immediate green light.

A 30+ VIX can mark a generational bottom (like 1997, 2011, or 2020) or it can be a devastating bull trap if credit and fundamentals are broken (like 2000 and 2008).

An update on something I’ve been messing around with given the recent market stress: a cross-asset regime model that asks a pretty simple question — when has the market looked like this before?

The latest reading is interesting. All 10 of the closest historical analogs are now stress / risk-off regimes, with October 2018 the closest match at 78% similarity.

October 2018 is an interesting comparison. Markets were dealing with rising Treasury yields, a more hawkish Fed, trade tensions and a pretty sharp reset in equity valuations — real market stress, but not a financial-system crisis.

That doesn’t mean today is 2018, or that we’re headed for a crisis. But the current mix across equities, rates, credit, volatility, FX and commodities is increasingly starting to resemble periods when markets were under meaningful pressure.

And maybe the most interesting part: what happened next in those historical periods was far from uniformly bearish.

posts.text:
An update on something I’ve been messing around with given the recent market stress: a cross-asset regime model that asks a pretty simple question — when has the market looked like this before?

The latest reading is interesting. All 10 of the closest historical analogs are now stress / risk-off regimes, with October 2018 the closest match at 78% similarity.

October 2018 is an interesting comparison. Markets were dealing with rising Treasury yields, a more hawkish Fed, trade tensions and a pretty sharp reset in equity valuations — real market stress, but not a financial-system crisis.

That doesn’t mean today is 2018, or that we’re headed for a crisis. But the current mix across equities, rates, credit, volatility, FX and commodities is increasingly starting to resemble periods when markets were under meaningful pressure.

And maybe the most interesting part: what happened next in those historical periods was far from uniformly bearish.

quoted.text:
Some fun: When has the market looked like this before?

I took the current cross-asset regime — equities, rates, credit, FX, commodities and volatility — and compared it with historical 63-trading-day periods based on both the direction and magnitude of market moves.

The closest historical match to November 2026?

April 2005 — 81% similarity.

What I found especially interesting is that it passes the macro smell test as well. Both periods combine relatively strong growth, elevated inflation, restrictive/tightening conditions, a fairly flat positive yield curve and credit markets that are not signaling acute stress.

That does not mean 2026 = 2005. There are some very important differences, particularly around housing and equity valuations.

So I also looked at what happened after the closest historical regimes.

Across the closest analogues, the median S&P 500 path was:

+2.0% after 1 month
+5.7% after 3 months
+3.4% after 6 months
+11.6% after 12 months
But the individual paths vary enormously — which is really the point.

Historical analogues aren't forecasts. They are a way of asking: when markets have been pricing a similar combination of growth, inflation, rates, credit and risk before, what happened next?

Still experimenting with this, but I think there is something pretty interesting here.

posts.text:
Over the past couple weeks we've met with management teams across memory, optics, neoclouds, semis, semi cap equipment and substrates.

Everyone is frustrated and confused about their stock prices but everyone is still very, very bullish.

Everyone expects 2027 capex to be significantly higher than 2026 and they expect 2028 capex to be moderately to significantly higher than 2027. 

Everyone knows the YoY capex growth rates will decelerate but the total dollars spent will continue to get bigger... at least for the next few years. Everyone says we're still in the early innings of ai adoption. 

Every company in the ai ecosystem is 50-100% sold out for 2027 and 40-80% sold out for 2028. 

Everyone is sitting on LTAs from the hyperscalers... some of those LTAs are getting signed and they last anywhere from 3 years to 6+ years... and they're getting done at record prices and record margins. Customers can't take the chance of not having enough supply to meet their needs over the next 3-5 years... locking up supply at record prices is better than not having enough supply when it's needed the most. 

Some of these LTAs could consume more than 50% of their supply over the next 2-3 years and at least one company has an LTA that would consume 75% of their capacity over the next 2-3 years. 

Neoclouds continue to see demand that is 5-10x higher than capacity. Many of them are saying the financing concerns are overblown. They're seeing 3-5 year deals get signed at 10-20% higher prices that the first half of 2026 and they think deals signed in the first half of 2027 will have 10-20% higher prices than deals signed in the second half of 2026. Power is still a big bottleneck and many sites are dealing with small construction delays but nothing is getting canceled. Customers are desperate for compute. Many of the neoclouds are trying to reserve 10-15% of capacity for shorter term deals and spot market because rates are 2-3x higher than the 3-5 year deals. 

Memory companies say demand will outstrip supply until 2029 at the earliest. They are very confident LTAs won't get cancelled because even at record prices for memory, the customers have enough margin to make it work. 

I know there's lots of fear and uncertainty in the market right now but it's not showing up in the demand... it remains stronger than ever... many backlogs are growing faster than current revenues.

In 20+ years of investing, I've honestly never seen this much dislocation between fundamentals and valuations. This is truly a historic time to be an investor and not in a good way. It's very hard to be patient and lean into your conviction/thesis during times like this but that's probably the right strategy for most long-term investors. 

Hopefully the lows are near. Make sure you are getting sleep, sunlight and exercise. Protect your mental health if possible.

posts.name: Michael A. Arouet
posts.text:
Everyone is scratching his head after the recent market sell-off, but it’s really not that complicated. It’s pure math. Let’s take a look, shall we?

At their peaks, the major listed AI-exposed companies (Mag7 plus key chip, foundry, and infrastructure names) were worth roughly $28–32 trillion. Add Anthropic’s post-IPO valuation of about $1.2–1.5 trillion and an expected OpenAI post-IPO figure around $1.5 trillion, and the total sits in the $30–35 trillion range, approaching half the entire US equity market (recently ~$70–72 trillion).

Once a single theme absorbed that much capital, further large gains required either massive new inflows or more money pulled from everything else. At some point neither was available at the necessary scale. Expecting these names to double again from those peaks implied an incremental $30+ trillion of market value. The rest of the US market was only ~$40 trillion; global equity markets, bonds, and private capital held no unused liquidity of that magnitude ready for AI multiples. Leverage, retail flows, and foreign capital were already heavily committed.

The arithmetic simply stopped working. Prices could no longer be justified by any realistic path of further capital absorption. The pullback was the delayed recognition that the liquidity sucked into the trade had nowhere left to come from. It’s really that simple. Seriously, what were people thinking buying these names at multi-trillion valuations? That they would double again in three months?

Imagine being the co-CEO of Alameda, buying a $2.5M yacht, quitting your job three months before FTX collapses and never spending a single day in prison.

That’s what happened to Sam Trabucco

probably one of the least talked about people in the entire FTX collapse 

Sam grew up in Natick, Massachusetts, the son of a police officer and a preschool teacher. 

He was obsessed with mathematics and puzzles from a very young age, and in 2008 he attended a mathematics summer camp where he met Gary Wang. Two years later, at the same camp, he met Sam Bankman-Fried.

They would eventually reunite at MIT, where Trabucco graduated in mathematics and computer science in 2015. 

He was also a poker and blackjack player who once joked about potentially being banned from three casinos, and even had crossword puzzles published in The New York Times.

After graduating, he joined Susquehanna International Group, one of the largest quantitative trading firms in the world. In 2017 he quit, moved to San Francisco and started trading crypto on his own because he realized he could make more money doing that than anything else.

In March 2019 he joined Alameda Research as a trader, and just two and a half years later, when SBF decided to focus entirely on FTX, he appointed Trabucco and Caroline Ellison as co-CEOs of Alameda.

By 2022, Sam was not even 30 years old and had already:

Made the Forbes 30 Under 30 list
Bought a $500K house in Maine
Bought a ~$9M apartment overlooking the Golden Gate Bridge
Bought a $2.5M yacht called “Soak My Deck”
Received $20M in cash during his time at Alameda, according to bankruptcy filings

But here we need to check the timing of his departure.

On August 24, 2022, he announced that he was stepping down as co-CEO of Alameda because he wanted to prioritize other things in his life. 

(He even mentioned that he had bought a boat and was enjoying it)

Less than three months later, FTX and Alameda went bankrupt.

Keep in mind that while Trabucco was still co-CEO, Alameda had accumulated $5.8B worth of FTT on a balance sheet of $14.6B, with only $134M in cash. 

He was also the person responsible for risk management, according to SBF’s testimony.

And while Caroline Ellison, Gary Wang and Nishad Singh pleaded guilty and SBF was sentenced to 25 years in prison, Trabucco was never criminally charged and didn’t even testify at Sam’s trial.

His last public tweet was on November 9, 2022, wishing everyone a brighter future after what had happened.

It’s been four years since that tweet.

Ok, I’m going to be as polite as possible even though I’m tired of explaining this. Forward earnings are horrible for assessing valuations when we’re at the end of the cycle.

Analysts extrapolate recent growth and elevated profit margins instead of anticipating mean reversion or recessionary contractions. As a result, the denominator in forward price to earnings ratios stay artificially high while the business cycle is already turning, making valuations appear more reasonable than trailing or cyclically adjusted ratios.

Students of financial history understand this. During the GFC, actual earnings collapsed about 92%, yet consensus estimates only fell about 6%. This disconnect happens at the end of every cycle and the beginning of every recession (although the GFC is an extreme example). Downward revisions to estimates only come after the damage is already visible.

posts.text:
Productivity, Not Rate Hikes, Tames Supercore!

Supercore inflation is no mystery, and it’s not a story about the federal funds rate. It is unit labor costs: pay minus productivity.

PCE supercore and nonfarm unit labor costs have a correlation of 0.82 since 1960, and 0.91 on two-year averages. In 2022, productivity fell 1.5%, unit labour costs rose 5.3%, and supercore peaked at 5.3% in October. In 2024, productivity rose 3.1% and unit labor  costs slowed to 2.0%, even as pay grew 5.1%. 

Supercore came down. The 1996 to 2004 boom worked the same way: productivity 3.1%, pay 4.4%, unit labor costs 1.3%, supercore 2.6%.

The only extended stretch when supercore held near 2% was post-GFC secular stagnation, from mid-2009 to early 2020. It averaged 2.1% and stayed in a 1.5% to 2.5% band in 82% of months, against 15% otherwise. It got there through weak pay of 2.5%, not a productivity boom.

Supercore has been above 2% in 88% of months since 1960, with a long-run average of 4.05%. It was 3.6% in September 2026. In the third quarter, unit labour costs were 2.4%, productivity 2.1% and pay 4.5%. Rate hikes do not create productivity. They cut the investment, including AI capex, that does.

A Fed that hikes into a productivity boom to chase a 2% supercore it has seen only in secular stagnation is not following the data. It is going rogue. The Fed should protect the productivity cycle, not choke it.
